doc_name: International Association for Engineering Geology and the Environment
text: The International Association for Engineering Geology and the Environment (IAEG), formerly known as the International Association for Engineering Geology, was founded in 1964 during the XXII International Geological Congress in New Delhi, where Israeli geologist Asher Shadmon proposed the creation of a permanent commission to address engineering geology, including the relationship between natural materials and engineering activities. On 17 December 1964, delegates unanimously voted to establish a Commission of "Engineering Geology" within the International Geological Congresses, with objectives to promote knowledge, gather case-histories, prepare literature reviews, collect statistical data, and identify further research needs. Due to resource limitations, a permanent commission was not formed, but instead a small committee led by Shadmon was created to assess the state of engineering geology by engaging with relevant international societies. On 21 December 1964, the International Association for Engineering Geology (IAEG) was officially established, with founding members including Marcel Arnould (France), G. Bain (USA), M.S. Balasundaram (India), L.M.C. Calembert (Belgium), R.S. Chaturvedi (India), G.C. Chowdhary (India), E. Beneo (Italy), K. Erguvanli (Turkey), A. Hamza (India), M.S. Jain (India), L.E. Kent (South Africa), V.S. Krishnaswamy (India), J.D.S. Lakshmaman (France), A.R. Mahendra (India), M. Manfredi (Italy), V. Prasad (India), B. Ramchandran (India), J.Th. Rosenqvist (Norway), B. Sanatkumar (India), P.B. Srinivasan (India), L.S. Srivastava (India), and M. Zapata (Spain). A provisional committee was elected to guide initial activities. By the end of 1966, the committee included Asher Shadmon (Israel) as president, Marcel Arnould (France) as secretary, E. Beneo (Italy), V.S. Krishnaswamy, R.S. Mithal, and M.S. Balasundaram (India), K. Erguvanli (Turkey), A.M. Hull (USA), E.M. Sergeev and N.V. Kolomenskij (USSR), Quido Záruba (Czechoslovakia), M.D. Ruiz (Brazil), and G. Champetier de Ribes (France) as treasurer. Discussions with representatives from Australia, Japan, and Mexico were ongoing. The association established its first statutes in the first two years, defining engineering geology as the application of earth sciences to engineering, planning, construction, prospecting, testing, and processing of materials, and setting aims to encourage research, training, and international cooperation. At the 1967 IUGS meeting, the IAEG requested affiliation, which was accepted by the executive committee and ratified unanimously by the IUGS general assembly on 23 August 1968 in Prague. The first general assembly was held in Prague in August 1968 during the XXIII IGC, despite political tensions, where the statutes were ratified and a four-year executive committee was elected. The new committee included Quido Záruba (Czechoslovakia) as president, Marcel Arnould (France) as secretary general, G. Champetier de Ribes (France) as treasurer, Asher Shadmon (Israel) as past president, L. Calembert (Belgium) as vice-president for Europe, L. Cluff (USA) for North America, M.D. Ruiz (Brazil) for South America, L. Oborn (New Zealand) for Australasia, H. Tanaka (Japan) for Asia, and a Ghanaian representative for Africa. Additional members included N.V. Kolomenskij (USSR), A. Nemock (Czechoslovakia), J. Janjic (Yugoslavia), R. Glossop (UK), A. Drucker (Federal Republic of Germany), and J.M. Crepeau (Canada). Three working groups were established, and it was decided to hold IAEG congresses alternately with the International Geological Congresses, allowing a general assembly every two years and scientific symposia in between. The first congress with a general assembly was in September 1970 in Paris, where the first edition of the Bulletin of the IAEG (later known as the Bulletin of Engineering Geology and the Environment) was distributed, edited by Quido Záruba, J. Pasek, and Marcel Arnould, and produced by the Paris School of Mines. The Bulletin became a respected scientific journal in engineering geology, the environment, and related geosciences and is now published by Springer Science+Business Media. In 1992, the general assembly in Kyoto approved updated statutes reflecting the field's growth, defining engineering geology as a science focused on investigating and solving engineering and environmental problems arising from human-geology interactions, predicting and preventing geologic hazards, and assessing the mechanical and hydrologic behavior of soil and rock masses, including their long-term property changes and stability parameters, as well as environmental condition improvements. As of December 2024, the IAEG has 4,857 members spread across 68 national groups (including one for Chinese Taipei). The IAEG organizes international congresses every four years, beginning in 1998 with a defined theme, and also holds regional conferences in Asia, South America, and Europe. The association operates with three goals: advancing engineering geology, improving teaching and training, and collecting, evaluating, and disseminating geological engineering results. It publishes the Bulletin of Engineering Geology and the Environment in collaboration with Springer Science+Business Media. The Hans Cloos Medal is awarded every two years to an engineering geologist of outstanding merit, and the IAEG congresses, such as the XII in Turin (Italy) in September 2014 and the XIII in San Francisco (California, USA) in September 2018, also serve as the 61st annual meeting of the Association of Environmental & Engineering Geologists. The IAEG is affiliated with the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) and is a member of the Federation of International Geo-Engineering Societies (FedIGS). The current president is Rafig Azzam from Aachen University of Technology.
